source_text: Τούτοις γὰρ δὴ πᾶσι τοῖς οὕτω τερπνοῖς ὁ κοινὸς ὑποκάθηται δυσμενὴς, ἀναμένων εἴ ποτε, τοῖς ὁρωμένοις δελεασθέντες, τῆς μὲν εὐ θείας ἐκτραπῶμεν ὁδοῦ, πρὸς δὲ τὸν ἐκείνου λόχον ἑαυτοὺς ἀποκλίνωμεν. Καὶ δέος πολὺ μή ποτε, προσ δραμόντες ἀφυλάκτως αὐτοῖς, καὶ τὴν ἐκ τῆς ἀπολαύσεως τέρψιν οὐδὲν ἡγησάμενοι βλαβερὸν, ἐγκεκρυμμένον τῇ πρώτῃ γεύσει τὸ τοῦ δόλου καταπίωμεν ἄγκιστρον· εἶτα ὑπὸ τούτου τὰ μὲν ἑκόντες, τὰ δὲ ἄκοντες, προσδεθῶμεν αὐτοῖς, καὶ πρὸς τὸ φοβερὸν τοῦ λῃστοῦ καταγώγιον τὸν θάνατον λάθωμεν ἑλκυσθέντες ὑπὸ τῶν ἡδονῶν. Ὥστε ἀναγκαῖον καὶ λυσιτελὲς ἅπασιν, ἀδελφοὶ, καθάπερ ὁδοιπόρους ἢ δρομέας στειλαμένους ἡμᾶς, καὶ πανταχόθεν τὸ κοῦφον ταῖς ψυχαῖς πρὸς τὸν δρό μον τοῦτον ἐπινοήσαντας, ἀμεταστρέπτως ἐπὶ τὸ τῆς ὁδοῦ πέρας ἐπείγεσθαι. Καί με μηδεὶς ὑπο λάβοι καινῶν ὀνομάτων γίνεσθαι ποιητὴν, ὅτι τὴν ἀνθρωπίνην ζωὴν ὁδὸν ἐκάλεσα νῦν, ἐπεὶ καὶ Δαβὶδ ὁ προφήτης οὕτω τὸν βίον ὠνόμασε· νῦν μὲν ὧδέ πη λέγων· Μακάριοι οἱ ἄμωμοι ἐν ὁδῷ, οἱ πορευό μενοι ἐν νόμῳ Κυρίου· νῦν δὲ πρὸς τὸν ἑαυτοῦ Δεσπότην βοῶν· Ὁδὸν ἀδικίας ἀπόστησον ἀπ' ἐμοῦ, καὶ τῷ νόμῳ σου ἐλέησόν με. Ποτὲ δὲ ὑμνῶν τὴν ὀξεῖαν τοῦ Θεοῦ κατὰ τῶν ἐπηρεαζόντων βοή θειαν, καὶ τῇ λύρᾳ προσάγων μεθ' ἡδονῆς, Καὶ τίς Θεὸς πλὴν τοῦ Θεοῦ ἡμῶν; ἔλεγεν· Ὁ Θεὸς ὁ περιζωννύων με δύναμιν, καὶ ἔθετο ἄμωμον τὴν ὁδόν μου· πανταχοῦ τὴν ἐπὶ γῆς τῶν ἀνθρώπων διατριβὴν, ἢ θαυμαζομένην ἢ φαύλην, οὕτω δεῖν προσαγορεύειν ἡγούμενος εἰκότως. Ὥσπερ γὰρ οἵ τινα συντεταμένην πορείαν ἀνύοντες, ἐπὶ τὰ πρόσω τὰς τῶν ποδῶν βάσεις ἁμιλλωμένας ἀλλήλαις εἰς δρόμον ἀμείβοντες, καὶ τὴν ἀεὶ προτέραν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς ἐρεισθεῖσαν δευτέραν ἀποδεικνύντες τῇ ταχείᾳ μεταθέσει τῆς ἄλλης, ῥᾳδίως ἐπὶ τὸ τῆς ὁδοῦ τέρμα χωροῦσιν· οὕτως οἱ πρὸς τὸ ζῇν παραχθέντες ὑπὸ τοῦ κτίσαντος, εὐθὺς ἐν ἀρχῇ τοῖς τοῦ χρόνου τμήμασιν ἐπεμβαίνοντες, καὶ τὸ πρότερον ἀεὶ καταλιμπάνοντες ὕστερον, ἐπὶ τὸ πέρας φθάνουσι τῆς ζωῆς. Ἢ οὐχὶ καὶ ὑμῖν δοκεῖ συνεχής τις ὁδὸς ὑφηπλῶσθαι ἡ παροῦσα ζωὴ, καὶ πορεία διειλημμένη ταῖς ἡλι κίαις καθάπερ σταθμοῖς, ἀρχὴν μὲν ἑκάστῳ τῆς ὁδοιπορίας παρέχουσα τὰς τῶν μητρῶν ὠδῖνας, τέρμα δὲ ὑποδεικνῦσα τοῦ δρόμου τὰς τῶν τάφων σκηνὰς, καὶ πρὸς ἐκείνας ἅπαντας ἄγουσα, τοὺς μὲν θᾶττον, τοὺς δὲ βραδύτερον, καὶ τοὺς μὲν διὰ πάν των τῶν τοῦ χρόνου διαστημάτων ὁδεύσαντας, τοὺς δὲ οὐδὲ τοῖς πρώτοις ἐναυλισθέντας τοῦ βίου σταθμοῖς; Τὰς μὲν οὖν ἄλλας ὁδοὺς, ὅσαι πρὸς πόλιν ἐκ πόλεως ἄγουσιν, ἔστιν ἐκκλῖναι, καὶ μὴ ὁδεῦσαι τὸν μὴ βουλόμενον· αὕτη δὲ, κἂν ἡμεῖς ἀναβάλλεσθαι βουληθῶμεν τὸν δρόμον, περιλαβοῦσα πρὸς βίαν, ἐπὶ τὸ τεταγμένον ὑπὸ τοῦ Δεσπότου πέρας ἕλκει τοὺς ἐπ' αὐτῆς· καὶ οὐκ ἔστιν, ἀγαπητοὶ, τὸν ἅπαξ ὑπεκδραμόντα τὴν ἐπὶ τόνδε τὸν βίον φέρουσαν πύλην, καὶ τῆς ὁδοῦ ταύτης ἐπιβάντα, μὴ καὶ πρὸς τὸ τέλος ταύτης ἐλθεῖν· ἕκαστος δὲ ἡμῶν, μετὰ τὸ τοὺς μητρῴους κόλπους ἀποφυγεῖν, εὐθὺς τοῖς τοῦ χρό νου ῥεύμασιν ἐνδεθεὶς ὑποσύρεται, κατόπιν ἀεὶ τὴν βεβιωμένην ἡμέραν ἐῶν, καὶ πρὸς τὴν χθὲς ἐπανελθεῖν οὐδέποτε, κἂν θελήσοι, δυνάμενος.
thought_title: Life as a road with the devil's hidden hook
orientation: Basil is warning his congregation that the devil hides beneath every worldly pleasure, and he now develops the image of human life as a road on which we must travel lightly.
pass_a_gloss: For under all these things so delightful the common enemy lies hidden, waiting to see if ever, baited by the things seen, we might turn aside from the divine road, and incline ourselves toward his ambush. And there is much fear lest ever, running to them unguardedly, and considering the enjoyment from the taking of pleasure in no way harmful, we swallow the hook of deceit hidden in the first taste; then by this, partly willingly, partly unwillingly, we might be bound to them, and toward the fearful lodging of the robber, death, we might be dragged unnoticed by the pleasures. So it is necessary and profitable for all, brothers, that we, like travelers or runners having prepared ourselves, and having devised from every side lightness for our souls for this race, press on without turning back to the end of the road. And let no one suppose that I am becoming a maker of new words, because I called human life a road just now, since also David the prophet so named life; at one time saying in this way: Blessed are the blameless in the road, those who walk in the law of the Lord; at another time crying to his own Master: Turn aside from me the road of unrighteousness, and by your law have mercy on me. And at another time hymning the swift help of God against those who insult, and bringing it to the lyre with pleasure, he said: And who is God except our God? The God who girds me with power, and he made my road blameless; everywhere considering that the sojourn of humans on earth, whether admired or base, must rightly be called so. For just as those who accomplish some shortened journey, changing the steps of their feet into a race toward the things ahead, the steps rivaling one another, and always showing the foot previously planted on the ground to be second by the swift transfer of the other, easily reach the end of the road; so those brought into life by the creator, immediately in the beginning stepping upon the segments of time, and always leaving behind the earlier for the later, arrive at the end of life. Or does not also to you the present life seem to be spread out as some continuous road, and a journey divided by the stages of life as by stopping-places, providing to each as the beginning of the journey the birth-pangs of mothers, and showing as the end of the race the tents of the tombs, and leading all toward those, some more quickly, some more slowly, and some having traveled through all the intervals of time, and others not even having lodged in the first stopping-places of life? The other roads, then, as many as lead from city to city, it is possible to turn aside from, and for the one not wishing it not to travel; but this one, even if we should wish to put off the race, having surrounded us by force, drags those on it toward the end appointed by the Master; and it is not possible, beloved, for the one who has once run out through the gate that leads to this life, and has set foot on this road, not also to come to its end; and each of us, after fleeing the maternal bosom, immediately bound in the streams of time is swept along, always leaving behind the day that has been lived, and never able to return to yesterday, even if he should wish it.

choices.why: The adjective 'common' marks the devil as the shared enemy of all humanity, and 'enemy' renders δυσμενής literally as one who is ill-disposed.

The source reads εὐ θείας with a space, but the intended word is εὐθείας, 'straight'; Basil's controlling image is the road of life, and 'divine' captures that this is the road God sets, though 'straight' is the literal sense.
The image is of a fishhook hidden in bait; 'hook of deceit' keeps the genitive of quality and the fishing metaphor Basil is building.
The word means a stopping-place or inn, but Basil uses it ironically for the robber's den; 'lodging' preserves the road-travel metaphor while allowing the sinister sense.
The middle voice of στέλλω means to get oneself ready or equipped for a journey; 'prepared ourselves' keeps the reflexive, deliberate preparation Basil urges.
The metaphor of σκηνή as tent or temporary dwelling is deliberate: tombs are the final stopping-places on the road, and 'tents' preserves the image of temporary shelter on a journey.

pass_b_english: Beneath all these things, however pleasant they seem, the common enemy lies hidden, waiting to see whether we will be baited by what we see, turn aside from the divine road, and lean toward his ambush. There is great reason to fear that we may run to these things without guarding ourselves, think that the enjoyment they give can do no harm, and swallow the hook of deceit concealed in the first taste. Then, partly willingly and partly against our will, we may be bound fast by them, and be dragged by pleasures to slip into that fearsome lodging of the robber, death. So it is necessary and profitable for everyone, brothers and sisters, to prepare ourselves like travelers or runners, to make our souls light in every way for this race, and to press on without turning back to the end of the road. Let no one suppose that I am inventing new terms because I have now called human life a road, since the prophet David also gave this name to life. At one point he says, “Blessed are those whose way is blameless, who walk in the law of the Lord” (Psalm 119:1). At another point he cries out to his Master, “Remove from me the way of falsehood, and be gracious to me by your law” (Psalm 119:29). And at another time, singing of God’s swift help against those who attack him and bringing it to the lyre with pleasure, he said, “For who is God except our God? The God who girds me with strength and made my way blameless” (Psalm 18:30-31). Everywhere he rightly considered that the time human beings spend on earth, whether admired or worthless, should be called by this name. For just as people who are completing a hurried journey move their feet forward, each step racing ahead of the other in a run, always making the foot previously planted on the ground second by the swift movement of the other, and so easily reach the end of the road, so those who have been brought into life by the Creator step immediately at the beginning onto the segments of time, always leaving behind the earlier segment for the later one, and arrive at the end of life. Or does it not seem to you as well that this present life is spread out like a continuous road, a journey divided by the stages of life as by stopping-places, giving to each person the birth-pangs of their mother as the beginning of the journey, and showing the tents of the tombs as the end of the race, and leading everyone to those tents, some more quickly and some more slowly, some traveling through all the intervals of time, and others not even lodging at the first stopping-places of life? Now the other roads, as many as lead from city to city, can be avoided, and the one who does not wish to travel them need not do so. But this road, even if we want to delay the race, surrounds us by force and drags those on it to the end appointed by the Master. And it is not possible, beloved, for the one who has once slipped out through the gate that leads into this life and set foot on this road not to come to its end. Each of us, after leaving our mother’s embrace, is immediately bound to the streams of time and swept along, always leaving behind the day we have lived and never able to return to yesterday, even if we wish to.
notes: The source text has εὐ θείας split across a line break; it is read as εὐθείας ('straight').
The source text has ὑπο λάβοι split across a line break; it is read as ὑπολάβοι.
The source text has πορευό μενοι split across a line break; it is read as πορευόμενοι.
The source text has βοή θειαν split across a line break; it is read as βοήθειαν.
The source text has ἡλι κίαις split across a line break; it is read as ἡλικίαις.
The source text has χρό νου split across a line break; it is read as χρόνου.

problems.quote: always making the foot that was planted on the ground before the second one
problems.source_quote: τὴν ἀεὶ προτέραν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς ἐρεισθεῖσαν δευτέραν ἀποδεικνύντες
problems.why: The syntax is garbled: 'making the previously planted foot second' (by the swift movement of the other).
problems.fix: always making the foot previously planted on the ground second

problems.why: φαύλην here means 'humble/base/ordinary', not 'wicked'; it's a contrast with admired, not moral judgment.
problems.ruling: φαύλην contrasts θαυμαζομένην as 'lowly/ordinary' vs 'admired'; 'wicked' imposes wrong moral sense.

problems.why: ὑπεκδραμόντα is 'slipped out/escaped from' the gate (birth), not 'passed through' neutrally.
problems.ruling: ὑπεκδραμόντα = 'run out from under/escape'; 'passed through' loses the forceful exit-from-birth imagery.

edits.old: always making the foot that was planted on the ground before the second one
edits.new: always making the foot previously planted on the ground second

fixed: Corrected garbled syntax: 'always making the foot previously planted on the ground second' matches 'τὴν ἀεὶ προτέραν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς ἐρεισθεῖσαν δευτέραν ἀποδεικνύντες'.
Changed 'wicked' to 'humble' for φαύλην, which here means 'base/ordinary' in contrast to 'admired', not morally wicked.
Changed 'passed through' to 'slipped out through' for ὑπεκδραμόντα, which means 'escaped/slipped out from' the gate of birth.

problems.why: φαύλην means 'worthless/bad', not 'humble'; the contrast is admired vs. despised.
problems.ruling: φαύλην means 'worthless/bad'; 'humble' misleads, breaking admired vs. despised contrast

problems.source_quote: Καὶ τίς Θεὸς πλὴν τοῦ Θεοῦ ἡμῶν; Ὁ Θεὸς ὁ περιζωννύων με δύναμιν, καὶ ἔθετο ἄμωμον τὴν ὁδόν μου
problems.why: This is Psalm 17:31-32 in LXX, which corresponds to Psalm 18:30-31 in Hebrew, not 18:31-32.
problems.ruling: LXX Ps 17:32 = Hebrew Ps 18:31; English '18:31-32' is off by one verse

fixed: Changed 'whether admired or humble' to 'whether admired or worthless' because φαύλην means 'worthless/bad', not 'humble'.
Changed 'Psalm 18:31-32' to 'Psalm 18:30-31' because the LXX Psalm 17:31-32 corresponds to Hebrew Psalm 18:30-31.

problems.why: λάθωμεν here means 'we may slip/escape (into death)' not 'without noticing'; it parallels καταγώγιον as the destination.
problems.fix: and slip into that fearsome lodging of the robber, death
problems.ruling: λάθωμεν is aorist subjunctive of λανθάνω 'escape notice'; 'without noticing it' inverts subject/object—Greek means 'we may unawares be dragged to death'.

edits.old: and be dragged by pleasures without noticing it to that fearsome lodging of the robber, death.
edits.new: and be dragged by pleasures to slip into that fearsome lodging of the robber, death.

fixed: Corrected λάθωμεν: the English 'without noticing it' misread the verb as an adverb; the source means 'we may slip/escape into death,' so the clause now reads 'to slip into that fearsome lodging of the robber, death.'

last_rejected.why: ὑποκάθηται means 'sits/lurks beneath', not 'lies hidden'; the enemy is seated in ambush.
last_rejected.fix: the common enemy sits in wait beneath
last_rejected.ruling: ὑποκάθηται: 'lies hidden' captures lurking beneath; 'sits beneath' is literal but same meaning.

last_rejected.fix: and in your law be gracious to me
last_rejected.ruling: 'by your law' is standard rendering of dative; 'in your law' equivalent meaning, not misleading.
